Corruption became a system — the Havana casino and tourist economy patronised by Meyer Lansky, with the Riviera Hotel opening in December 1957 — while repression escalated from censorship and torture to mass killing after the Cienfuegos naval rising of 5 September 1957, leaving an estimated 10,000–20,000 dead by 1959. Each act manufactured enemies: the murder of Frank País, the bombing of rebel-held hamlets and the refusal to hold honest elections drove the middle class, the Church and eventually Washington away. His army of some 40,000 was a patronage machine, and the April 1958 conspiracy of Colonel Ramón Barquín, uncovered and punished, showed that even his officer corps doubted him. Economically, dependence on the US sugar quota, rural unemployment and the 1958 recession made his claim to order and prosperity implausible. Above all he refused the compromise that might have saved him: he blocked a provisional government, staged the fraudulent election of 3 November 1958 that installed Andrés Rivero Agüero, and — after the US arms embargo of 14 March 1958 and Washington's search for a military junta — chose flight over resistance on 1 January 1959, handing Havana to Castro rather than to a caretaker junta. The post-revisionist school reads this sequence as decisive. Batista's weaknesses were not one factor among five but the catalyst that activated the others: his illegitimacy supplied the propaganda, his army's decay supplied the guerrilla victories, his intransigence supplied the united opposition, and his dependence supplied the lever for American pressure. The extent of his responsibility is therefore primary.\n\n### Support from other countries (≈310 words)\n\nExternal support mattered, but not in the way Cold War narratives imply: the decisive international variable was the erosion, not the arrival, of foreign backing. Batista had been armed and trained by the United States under Mutual Defense Assistance programmes, and the US military mission in Havana symbolised his external guarantee; when Washington suspended arms shipments on 14 March 1958, wound up its military mission, and by November–December 1958 pressed for a junta and sent William Pawley on a mediation mission, Batista's air force and armour lost the spare parts and bombs that sustained them, and his political survival lost its main external prop. Castro's international assets before 1959 were symbolic rather than material: Matthews's articles of February 1957 made the Sierra a global story and deterred decisive repression; arms and recruits were bought in Mexico and the United States by exile committees, the *Granma* being purchased near Mexico City in 1956 and the expedition trained by the Spanish Civil War veteran Alberto Bayo; foreign fighters such as the Argentine Guevara gave the Movement prestige; and sympathetic Latin American governments, notably Venezuela's, offered quiet encouragement. Crucially there was no Soviet or Chinese aid, and Cuba's communists (the PSP) dismissed the Sierra as \"putschist\" until mid-1958 — Moscow had no role in Castro's victory. The asymmetry is telling: the side with a superpower patron lost. For the post-revisionist school this confirms that legitimacy and domestic coalition-building, not external sponsorship, decided the war, and it answers the question by showing that foreign support operated entirely through Batista's weaknesses, since his dependence made him vulnerable to American pressure. The extent of this factor's responsibility is significant, but chiefly as the final removal of Batista's remaining prop.\n\n### United opposition (≈305 words)\n\nThe united opposition was broad but never genuinely unified, and its cohesion was produced by Batista's refusal to permit any legal exit. The anti-Batista field included Castro's 26th of July Movement; the Directorio Revolucionario, whose assault on the Presidential Palace on 13 March 1957 killed its leader José Antonio Echeverría and which opened a second front in the Escambray in late 1957; the Auténticos and Ortodoxos; and the Communist PSP, which condemned the Sierra until Carlos Rafael Rodríguez visited it in July 1958. Because Batista blocked elections and dialogue, these groups converged: the Catholic hierarchy's pastoral letters and the Civic Dialogue of 1958 legitimised opposition among the middle class; the Caracas Pact of 20 July 1958 bound Castro, Miró Cardona, Justo Carrillo and Aureliano Sánchez Arango to a common front and a provisional government; and the failure of the 9 April 1958 general strike shifted authority from the urban *llano* to the Sierra, enabling Castro's \"total war\" proclamation of 1 May 1958. Castro then outmanoeuvred his allies, denouncing the Miami Pact of 1 November 1958 and imposing Manuel Urrutia as provisional president, so that the coalition's unity channelled power to him. The post-revisionist school reads this as the revolution's real mechanism: a civic front, not a foco, brought Batista down. Batista's weaknesses were the catalyst here too, since only his repression and intransigence could have united Liberals, Catholics, communists and students behind a thirty-two-year-old guerrilla. The extent of responsibility is therefore high: without Batista's closure of political space the opposition would plausibly have fragmented into negotiation, and Castro would have remained one faction
